content: This is the space for discussing graph definitions in this PR.
I will maintain my stance from the prior PR that this is a mistake. I have made this mistake before.
Also CC @Bhavik Mehta
Please focus on the content of the PRs.
I have addressed it already
Please check the prior PR
We explicitly addressed concerns raised in that PR (#427).
I hope to see someone from the mathlib side suggest that this duplication of API is justified.
Personally, as someone who knows how to write graph algorithms in lean, I see no reason to do so. The particular maintenance concerns raised previously have not been addressed.
Other unaddressed concerns include the lack of integration with order theory classes. But that is of tertiary importance. The unnecessary duplication is by far the bigger issue.
The Design. paragraph is dedicated to the motivation of this duplication.

It might be less bad if Mathlib adopts GraphLike (#36743), then alternative representations of graphs are fair game and make sense, without having to duplicate any API. I'd love to see stuff like using adjacency lists, or binary trees, all using Mathlib's graph API.

Basil Rohner said:

The Design. paragraph is dedicated to the motivation of this duplication.

I am aware. I am just saying the justification provided is

  1. Very insufficient
  2. Doesn’t do an analysis of the tech debt and maintenance costs entailed.

Further, I am emphasising the lack of necessity of duplication. Writing graph algorithms in the existing api is not a challenge, one can get the adjacency set representation trivially from SimpleGraph and digraph and then write algorithms with it. Further there is a huge deal of work in adjacency and incidence matrices as well as laplacians. All this is more than sufficient to write graph algorithms.
If you wish to duplicate API you must duplicate all the (tens of?) thousands of lines of API and then maintain them in sync with upstream.

Our graph definition is based on edge and vertex sets, which is the natural representation for the combinatorics we formalize. The adjacency relation is straightforwardly recoverable. One doesn't need to duplicate Mathlib's formalized results, one can we show equivalence between our definition and Mathlib's, then carry over the necessary theorems.
I am saying you should go the other way around

Thanks for opening a thread to discuss.

I tend to agree that redefining things that exist already in Mathlib is a last resort. We did this for instance for automata, which I think is a legitimate generalization in a mostly inactive and relatively small area of Mathlib.

I'm less familiar here, but this seems like a very different situation, where there's active development and much more existing work. I'd really like to hear the opinions of Mathlib contributors to this area.

I hold the strong opinion that domain-specific definitions are a worthwhile trade-off: they make the actual formalization, which is the bulk of the work, significantly more efficient, even if bridging back to Mathlib requires additional effort. This is especially true when the goal is formalizing modern, complex results. The definitions need to be close to the conventional ones used in informal mathematics and simple enough to avoid unnecessary overhead. Both criteria are difficult to meet with Mathlib's current graph API.
@Basil Rohner I am saying you need strong justification for the claim that mathlib API is inadequate. There is none so far.
And to add. This is a newbie mistake I made in 2024 for distributed graph algorithms.

When you work with mathlib API you have not just the direct graph theory api, but also the API of the underlying structures. The API lemmas and typeclasses have been designed to work in concert. Thus simp and grind lemmas are stated at the right level of generality and reusability. This makes a substantial difference in proof size and quality. To wit, if you check discord, you might see some of my old graph definitions which match yours. I actually recall showing them to Sorrachai back then. And you might also find algorithms I wrote. Thankfully Bhavik showed me how effective and simple my algorithms and proofs were by just reusing the mathlib version.

Basil Rohner said:

This is especially true when the goal is formalizing modern, complex results. The definitions need to be close to the conventional ones used in informal mathematics and simple enough to avoid unnecessary overhead. Both criteria are difficult to meet with Mathlib's current graph API.

I disagree strongly here. Particularly for graph theory, the definitions are close to the conventional ones used in informal mathematics, and don't have significant overhead. As a result, mathlib's graph theory has already been used to formalise modern, complex results: #general > Lean in the wild @ 💬, #maths > A recent proof about Ramsey numbers @ 💬.
That is, both criteria are already met, and demonstrably so, more than in most areas of mathematics and mathlib.

As for algorithms, I am actually working on those right now, and I am following the strategy I suggested above. Mathlib already provides you the adjacency matrix of a graph. Deducing the adjacency list structure is trivial with neighborSet and neighborFinset.

I admit it doesn’t help that I haven’t made them public yet, but in my defense Algolean is just a month old and I have gotten a lot of interest on the complexity theory side.
How do you reason over multi-graphs with SimpleGraph for example?
You don't, you use Mathlib's docs#Graph

Was just about to say that. Further your PR says you are also reinventing SimpleGraph and Digraph

SimpleGraph: finite undirected graph without loops or multi-edges
DiGraph: (possibly infinite) directed graph

The reason that we introduce those notions at once is that they work well together. By making the vertex and edge set explicit in all definitions the definition of a graph Graph is compatible with the definition of a simple graph SimpleGraph, allowing general results to be carrier over to more specialized structures. That's not the case with Mathlib's definition. This is to point out that Mathlib's SimpleGraph is insufficient (which was claimed above).

I think there are several layers of misunderstanding to be addressed here.

  1. Yes we all know vertex sets would be nice to have across all graph definitions. There is ongoing to work to add them to mathlib definitions (including a bit of my own).
  2. Mathlib graphs have edge sets. So you are wrong about this point.
    (More points coming please wait)
For 2. SimpleGraph is not defined in terms of an edge set (which is the point: Graph is while SimpleGraph is not).
1. That’s not a relevant point. One can deduce this edgeSet.

1. The way to address a perceived deficiency in mathlib APIs is to discuss in the #graph theory channel and then make the agreed upon PRs. Doing so ensures coherence of definitions. Further you still benefit from all the APIs that exist.
  2. Writing your own definitions and writing equivalence theorems to the mathlib definition does not automatically mean you can reuse all theorems from mathlib. We are not in the world of HoTT, where proofs are transported along equivalences.

You can get the edge set of a simple graph (docs#SimpleGraph.edgeSet) and build a simple graph from its edge set (docs#SimpleGraph.fromEdgeSet). It's a well-understood Lean pattern to do things like this, in all areas of mathematics.

1. Once you write code and put them in a library like CSLib, the community commits to maintaining the definitions. This is extra work. For duplicated definitions, keeping things coherent multiplies this work. So the justification for duplicating APIs has to be much stronger than “Oh we don’t want to use the api definition that does exactly what we ask”. That’s to say the justification has to be something like “we tried to write this code in lean. We asked all the experts on Zulip. The conclusion is that the current definitions are inadequate to express this concept and the existing mathlib definition cannot be altered”. This is a very high bar to meet. You’d actually have to show code, get expert feedback which backs your case, and show that you can’t make any upstream changes to improve the situation.
The second conjunct in the reasoning is very important
Hi, I am working on building APIs for Graph in Mathlib. I would be happy to collaborate if anything is not accommodating enough for the CS side!
Yes, I think a much more productive way forward here would be to improve Mathlib, rather than throwing it out!

Concretely you might perceive three concerns with existing API.

  1. Vertex sets. Feel free to discuss and adopt #33466 . Do please check first with @Alena Gusakov who wanted to adopt it. It has already been golfed. It just stayed in review long enough to acquire merge conflicts.
  2. Finite sets and adjacency collections(finsets/lists). Here mathlib already has you covered.
  3. SimpleGraph is not a specialization of Digraph and Digraph is not a specialization of Graph. This is all work-in-progress. Fixing this in mathlib is the more effective course of action.

Jun Kwon said:

Hi, I am working on building APIs for Graph in Mathlib. I would be happy to collaborate if anything is not accommodating enough for the CS side!

For reference, the proposed CSLib definition of a general undirected multigraph is:

structure Graph (α ε : Type*) where
  /-- The set of vertices. -/
  vertexSet : Set α
  /-- The set of edges. -/
  edgeSet : Set ε
  /-- The endpoint map, sending each edge to its unordered pair of endpoints. -/
  endpoints : ε → Sym2 α
  /-- Every endpoint of an edge is a vertex. -/
  incidence : ∀ e ∈ edgeSet, ∀ v ∈ endpoints e, v ∈ vertexSet

Whereas Mathlib's Graph is:

structure Graph (α β : Type*) where
  /-- The vertex set. -/
  vertexSet : Set α
  /-- The binary incidence predicate, stating that `x` and `y` are the ends of an edge `e`.
  If `G.IsLink e x y` then we refer to `e` as `edge` and `x` and `y` as `left` and `right`. -/
  IsLink : β → α → α → Prop
  /-- The edge set. -/
  edgeSet : Set β := {e | ∃ x y, IsLink e x y}
  /-- If `e` goes from `x` to `y`, it goes from `y` to `x`. -/
  isLink_symm : ∀ ⦃e⦄, e ∈ edgeSet → (Symmetric <| IsLink e)
  /-- An edge is incident with at most one pair of vertices. -/
  eq_or_eq_of_isLink_of_isLink : ∀ ⦃e x y v w⦄, IsLink e x y → IsLink e v w → x = v ∨ x = w
  /-- An edge `e` is incident to something if and only if `e` is in the edge set. -/
  edge_mem_iff_exists_isLink : ∀ e, e ∈ edgeSet ↔ ∃ x y, IsLink e x y := by exact fun _ ↦ Iff.rfl
  /-- If some edge `e` is incident to `x`, then `x ∈ V`. -/
  left_mem_of_isLink : ∀ ⦃e x y⦄, IsLink e x y → x ∈ vertexSet := by grind

Mathlib's design essentially lifts the Adj relation from SimpleGraph by adding an edge label, then moves the edge set in the definition, which requires the additional fields isLink_symm, eq_or_eq_of_isLink_of_isLink, edge_mem_iff_exists_isLink, and left_mem_of_isLink. In the proposed definition these properties are either immediate from Sym2 (symmetry, endpoint uniqueness) or captured directly by incidence, so no additional proof obligation.

I'd be interested to hear a concrete reason why the proposed formulation would be insufficient, given that it carries the same data with less overhead.

That’s a good starting point. There is an ongoing topic in #graph theory for this. Would be worthwhile discussing there and contributing to mathlib. Mathlib adopts the more general notion of having a separate edge type.
I don't think your def of Graph is insufficient. They are both capable of modelling (multi)graphs. From what I gather from @Peter Nelson is that relation are easier to work with in proofs.
I made some comments in cslib#503. In particular, @Basil Rohner , can't you define the API endpoints and incidence on mathlib's Graph?
Those two definitions are mathematically equivalent. But does the current definition of Graph cause pain points for CS? If so, what are they? Could you tell us?

Jun Kwon said:

I don't think your def of Graph is insufficient. They are both capable of modelling (multi)graphs. From what I gather from Peter Nelson is that relation are easier to work with in proofs.

Working with Graph (possible less than @Peter Nelson ) I think the definition is less convenient to work with. The endpoints formulation into Sym2 α gives you symmetry and endpoint uniqueness structurally, for free, whereas IsLink recovers these properties only through the proof obligations isLink_symm and eq_or_eq_of_isLink_of_isLink, which must be discharged every time you construct a Graph.

The adjacency relation:

def Adj (G : Graph α ε) (u v : α) : Prop :=
  ∃ e ∈ G.edgeSet, G.endpoints e = s(u, v)

It's symmetric by construction, since s(u, v) = s(v, u). No additional lemma needed. Incidence is similarly direct:

def Inc (G : Graph α ε) (e : ε) (v : α) : Prop :=
  e ∈ G.edgeSet ∧ v ∈ G.endpoints e

TLDR: I'd argue that all that IsLink provides is recoverable, but the endpoints formulation avoids encoding a function as a relation and then axiomatically reconstructing the properties that the function would have given you definitionally. Additionally for further extensions, such as Hypergraphs one could simply take the proposed definition and replace Sym2 with Set: 

structure Hypergraph (α ε : Type*) where
  /-- The set of vertices. -/
  vertexSet : Set α
  /-- The set of edges. -/
  edgeSet : Set ε
  /-- The endpoint map, assigning to each edge its set of incident vertices. -/
  endpoints : ε → Set α
  /-- Every endpoint of an edge is a vertex. -/
  incidence : ∀ e ∈ edgeSet, ∀ v ∈ endpoints e, v ∈ vertexSet

The additional fields needed to enforce the constraints form additional overhead in formalization.

By "additional fields", do you mean the current def requires more mathematical constraints? It doesn't, both defs are equivalent. Or do you mean that the number of fields is longer like 4 vs 7? We can easily make a constructor for Graph that takes in your def as input.
With the right aesop_graph annotations you might not even need the specialized .mk def

As the PR author of the current mathlib Graph, I’ll mention that the reason for using relations over functions in the definition is so that DecidableEq stays out of type signatures as much as possible. Possibly this is an issue for someone doing computations rather than proving theorems, but nothing above seems to suggest that.

Other than that, the mathlib definition is equivalent to the proposed one mathematically, so there shouldn’t be any ergonomic differences that can’t be solved without eg. alternative constructors. But others have already said this.

Basil Rohner said:

which must be discharged every time you construct a Graph.

I want to mention that you're meant to create new constructors that are best for particular applications. The main constructor is the low-level interface that guarantees we all agree on what the data of a graph is.

Using relations like this is a way to make the definition take as few assumptions as possible, and to be relatively easy to discharge for the basic API. Yes, things can factor through Sym2, but it's nice to avoid quotient types when you can (as Peter said, it imposes DecidableEq in places due to the fact factoring through Sym2 means things have to be computable Lean functions). I'm saying this as the original author of Sym2 that things can get painful if you make it part of your definition.

Another thing: I thought I'd mention something about SimpleGraph, since it seems to be often misunderstood. The point of SimpleGraph is to be the abstract interface for your concrete types for simple graphs — a simple graph after all is, extensionally, just its adjacency relation. You define your own graph type, create a function to SimpleGraph, prove that function is injective, and there you go, you can use the SimpleGraph API on it (once you prove enough theorems about this function you created). It could be more seamless of course.

For this particular use case you can instantiate or build constructors for Mathlib’s SimpleGraph, Digraph, and Graph instead of writing your own definitions. This is exactly what others have also said. Kyle is also referring to specialized graph types broadly speaking. Graph algorithms are supposed to work on all instantiations of SimpleGraphs, Digraphs, and Graphs.

In your formalisation duplication will be necessary. You are already duplicating definitions. Further you have provided no justification that your definitions make proof in algorithms simpler. I am quite certain they don’t. Moving proofs across equivalences is not trivial. For what it is worth, I’d like to see some examples where you work with mathlib’s SimpleGraph and your version, preferably with proofs of correctness that you claim to be easy in your definitions. This claim still sticks out without any evidence, and stands contrary to my experience.

Secondly, in this particular instance, such constructors are better placed in mathlib. Some of them already exist as Bhavik pointed out. Reinventing them is also duplication. In the case of vertex sets (which is the only limitation you point out that might be a drawback at present), I suggest working with mathlib. Adopting #33466 would be a good starting point. The rest of the definitional structure you provide already exists as API.

@Basil Rohner , it seems like you are repeatedly making a point about the merits of one definition of graph over another, but whether or not this is true is at cross purposes with what others are saying.

To make this a little more concrete, here is what the kind of 'alternative constructor' API being mentioned would look like. 

import Mathlib.Combinatorics.Graph.Basic

variable {α β : Type*}

namespace Graph

/-- Define endpoints in terms of the data in `Graph`.
Probably needs some decidability to define correctly.  -/
def endpoints [DecidableEq α] (G : Graph α β) (e : β) : Sym2 α := sorry

/-- Provided `Graph.endpoints` has been defined correctly, the following lemma will be provable. -/
@[simp]
lemma mem_endpoints_iff [DecidableEq α] {G : Graph α β} {x : α} {e : β} :
  x ∈ G.endpoints e ↔ G.Inc e x := sorry

/-- An alternative constructor for `Graph` given an `endpoints` function. -/
def mkEndpoints (vertexSet : Set α) (edgeSet : Set β) (endpoints : β → Sym2 α)
    (incidence : ∀ e ∈ edgeSet, ∀ v ∈ endpoints e, v ∈ vertexSet) : Graph α β where
  vertexSet := vertexSet
  IsLink e u v := (endpoints e = Sym2.mk u v)
  isLink_symm := sorry
  eq_or_eq_of_isLink_of_isLink := sorry
  edge_mem_iff_exists_isLink := sorry
  left_mem_of_isLink := sorry

/-- `mkEndpoints` builds a graph with the right `endpoints`.-/
@[simp]
lemma mkEndpoints_endpoints [DecidableEq α] (vertexSet : Set α) (edgeSet : Set β)
    (endpoints : β → Sym2 α) (incidence) :
    (mkEndpoints vertexSet edgeSet endpoints incidence).endpoints = endpoints := sorry

Once the above sorrys are filled in (and this only needs to happen once), you can build a mathlib Graph in terms of an endpoints function, and never use Graph.mk again. It is then not matter of the merits of one definition over another - the API can exist both for thinking of a graph in terms of endpoints, or in terms of an incidence predicate, and everything you can do with one definition can be done equally with the other definition, with no need for a translation layer at all; you are working with Graph either way.

To make another point: there is an actual issue with your proposed definition, which comes from the choice of a function over a relation. Here is the definition again, for reference. 

structure Graph (α ε : Type*) where
  /-- The set of vertices. -/
  vertexSet : Set α
  /-- The set of edges. -/
  edgeSet : Set ε
  /-- The endpoint map, sending each edge to its unordered pair of endpoints. -/
  endpoints : ε → Sym2 α
  /-- Every endpoint of an edge is a vertex. -/
  incidence : ∀ e ∈ edgeSet, ∀ v ∈ endpoints e, v ∈ vertexSet

The issue is that the definition contains junk data; if e is not an element of edgeSet, then endpoints e still needs to be defined, even though it is mathematically meaningless. In particular, this means that Graph has a bad equality predicate; you can have terms G H : Graph α β that represent the same graph mathematically, but for which G ≠ H, because G and H differ on junk data.

It is also impossible to define an empty graph of type Graph α β, if α is an empty type but β is nonempty. This may seem like a trivial concern, but will potentially cause some friction and mathematically unnecessary nonemptiness assumptions.

I have to say that I'm almost convinced, thank you very much for the patience. I will think about it more.

In fact, the junk data also causes issues with the definition of endpoints from Graph in the first place. Probably endpoints needs to have type (e : β) → (h : e ∈ edgeSet) → Sym2 α to fix all this.

edit : I wrote this not having seen your reply above, which I'm glad to see!
you could resolve this junk value issue by turning endpoints into a predicate and then you won't have the proof obligation h either. But then you are getting closer to Peter's definition.

Something roughly like the following:

structure Graph (α ε : Type*) where
  /-- The set of vertices. -/
  vertexSet : Set α
  /-- The set of edges. -/
  edgeSet : Set ε
  /-- The endpoint map, sending each edge to its unordered pair of endpoints. -/
  isEndpoint : ε → α → Prop
  /-- Every endpoint of an edge is a vertex. -/
  -- commented out for simplicity. Adapt as required. incidence : ∀ e ∈ edgeSet, ∀ v ∈ endpoints e, v ∈ vertexSet

def endpointPointSet (edge : ε) : Set α := {w : α | Graph.isEndpoint edge w}

This trivially generalizes to hypergraphs.

I considered almost exactly this definition with the original PR. (isEndpoint is called Inc in the current API). Of course you get the same data as IsLink, but IsLink turned out to be a little more explicit in a way that helped with basic API. For instance, because of technicalities involving loops, it is a lot cleaner to write Inc in terms of IsLink than the other way around - see docs#Graph.isLink_iff_inc

Of course, it doesn't matter which is used!

Agreed. Also thanks for providing a concrete example of what constructor functions look like. Bhavik already linked to mathlib examples for SimpleGraphs, and I assumed this would be sufficient. But sometimes having a concrete code example inside the discussion thread is helpful.

The discussion so far appears to confirm my initial assessment that a duplication of mathlib API (i.e. new definitions of Graphs) is not justified in this case, and helping build mathib's API is the better option here.
I think API for an endpoints function on Graph would be welcome.

Quite incidentally turning endpoint into a prop resolves a conundrum I had where I wanted a view subgraph which contains half-edges (w.r.t to the vertices of the subgraph of course). I am quite certain this issue will arise again when I touch graph cuts, clusterings, and decompositions.

Shreyas Srinivas said:

I believe Kyle is saying something different and more general

No, this is overgeneralizing. There is no harm in creating a new structure for specific kinds of graph data. In fact, for algorithms, I would expect new structures, since the algorithms would compute on these structures, possibly even constructing new graphs during evaluation. The abstract interfaces are unsuitable for that.

Think of it this way: if you have a custom SimpleGraph.mkFromSuchAndSuchData constructor, you can curry it and have it take a single structure argument collecting all the necessary fields. There's no reason not to do this.

Shreyas Srinivas said:

Moving proofs across equivalences is not trivial.

Peter Nelson said:

To make another point: there is an actual issue with your proposed definition, which comes from the choice of a function over a relation. Here is the definition again, for reference. 

structure Graph (α ε : Type*) where
  /-- The set of vertices. -/
  vertexSet : Set α
  /-- The set of edges. -/
  edgeSet : Set ε
  /-- The endpoint map, sending each edge to its unordered pair of endpoints. -/
  endpoints : ε → Sym2 α
  /-- Every endpoint of an edge is a vertex. -/
  incidence : ∀ e ∈ edgeSet, ∀ v ∈ endpoints e, v ∈ vertexSet

The issue is that the definition contains junk data; if e is not an element of edgeSet, then endpoints e still needs to be defined, even though it is mathematically meaningless. In particular, this means that Graph has a bad equality predicate; you can have terms G H : Graph α β that represent the same graph mathematically, but for which G ≠ H, because G and H differ on junk data.

It is also impossible to define an empty graph of type Graph α β, if α is an empty type but β is nonempty. This may seem like a trivial concern, but will potentially cause some friction and mathematically unnecessary nonemptiness assumptions.
